title: Why Kaliya Took Refuge in the Yamuna
story:
There was a question the whole affair left behind, and it would not let the mind go. When the serpent had been sent away, the king who was listening to the tale asked it aloud: how had Kaliya, a king among serpents, ever come to live in the Yamuna at all? For it explained the strangest part of what they had just witnessed — why so great a serpent had cowered in a village river instead of reigning in the ocean where his kind belonged. And the sage answered him, and told of an old quarrel and an older curse.

In those days the serpents owed a share to Garuda. At every change of the moon they were to bring him his portion, and Garuda, the golden eagle who is dear to the Lord, came and took what was his. The serpents and the eagle had been enemies since the world was young; the tribute was the price of peace, the portion that kept the great bird from falling upon them all. But Kaliya was proud of his own poison, and drunk on the strength of it he withheld the tribute, and gave nothing.

When Garuda heard of it he was furious. He came upon Kaliya with the speed of a storm, for he was the very carrier of Vishnu, and no serpent in the world could match him. The serpent rose to meet him with his many heads raised, venom as his weapon, but the son of Tarkshya was not deterred. He struck with his left wing, the wing that shone like gold, and Kaliya, the son of Kadru, was beaten and dazed, and fled in terror.

He fled to a pool in the Yamuna, and there he found safety, and the safety was not of his own making. Long before, Garuda had come to that very spot wanting to eat a fish, and the sage Saubhari, who dwelt there, had seen the fish in their distress when their king was devoured. Out of compassion he had laid a curse: if ever Garuda entered that pool again, his life would end. So the great eagle kept away from the water, and Kaliya — alone among all the serpents, for only he knew the story — took refuge there, in the one place the eagle could not follow.

And so the poison in the river had a deeper root than anyone in Vrindavan knew. The serpent in their water was not merely cruel; he was a fugitive who had once defied the mightiest bird in the world and fled to the only place on earth where that bird could not come. He had turned his fear into a kingdom, and the river had paid for it.
reflection: The backstory quietly reverses what the villagers must have seen. Kaliya was not simply the monster in their water but a fugitive who had defied Garuda and fled to the one place the eagle could not enter. His tyranny was fear hardened into a kingdom, and the river paid the price.
next_story_tease: The serpent was gone now; only the boy remained in the water, and the people waiting on the bank.
hero_scene: Garuda, the golden eagle, striking the many-headed Kaliya with his shining left wing as the serpent rears to meet him, water and sky churning around them.
